title: Wells without power
summary: With no power an electric well pump stops: use stored water, the pressure tank, a hand pump or a safely run generator. After a flood, don’t use the well until it is disinfected and tested.
doFirst: Flood water reached the well? Don’t drink, cook, bathe or wash with its water.
Turn off the power to the well before you touch anything. Never step in water around a well unless you are sure the power is off.
Run a generator only outdoors, more than 20 ft (6 m) from windows, doors and vents.

list: An electric well pump can’t pump water without power (Private Well Class, University of Illinois and RCAP, funded by EPA).
Turn off the power to the pump at the breaker so it doesn’t start on its own when the power comes back, and label that breaker (Private Well Class).
If your pressure tank has a faucet near the bottom, you can draw water from it (Private Well Class). Treat it before drinking if you are not sure the well is safe.
Use your stored water (Water Systems Council).
When the power comes back, make sure it is fully restored before you start the pump (Private Well Class).
A generator can run the well pump (Water Systems Council).

A qualified electrician should install the generator and a transfer switch. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet: power can feed back into the lines and endanger line workers and anyone near downed lines (University of Illinois Extension).
Never use a generator inside your home or garage, even with doors and windows open. Run it outside, more than 20 feet (6 m) from any window, door or vent (CDC).
Use a battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide detector in the house while it runs (CDC).
Turn it off and let it cool before you refuel it (University of Illinois Extension).
Keep it dry: a generator is an electrical risk when wet (University of Illinois Extension).
A hand pump fitted to the well keeps water coming in a long outage (Water Systems Council). Have it installed before you need it.

With no pump at all, water can be bailed out of a well with a bucket or other device (CDC, in its well disinfection steps). A drilled well’s casing can be only a few inches wide (CDC’s tables start at 2 inches), so the bucket must be narrow enough to fit.
Working on a well after a disaster can be hazardous; CDC says it should be done by a well or pump contractor.

blocks.warn: Never enter a well pit: gases and vapors can build up in it (CDC).

blocks.p: If flood water reached the well, don’t drink, cook, bathe or wash with its water (EPA) until it has been disinfected and tested (CDC). A flooded well may not be safe for many months (EPA).

list: Turn off all electricity to the well before you clear debris (CDC). Never step in water around a well unless you are sure the power is off (NYS Department of Health). Rubber boots and gloves do not protect you from electric shock (EPA).
Watch for power lines on the ground or in the water, sharp debris, open holes and slippery ground (CDC).
Don’t turn the pump on until a qualified electrician, well contractor or pump contractor has checked the wiring (CDC, EPA).
If the water smells of fuel or chemicals, don’t use it: boiling or disinfecting won’t make it safe (CDC, NYS Department of Health).

In normal times, call your local health department before using the well again (CDC, NYS Department of Health). In New York, NYS Department of Health says to use other water until the health department says otherwise.

blocks.p: CDC says a well or pump contractor should do this. If none can come, these are CDC’s steps. Wear goggles or a face shield, work where there is fresh air and don’t breathe the vapors. Tell everyone not to drink or bathe in the water until every step is done (CDC).

blocks.warn: Don’t climb down into a well. Bleach gives off chlorine gas; WHO says anyone who must enter a well needs full protective clothing and a breathing apparatus, so clean the lining from the top with a long-handled brush (WHO).

blocks.p: Use only plain, unscented household liquid chlorine bleach, usually 5% to 9% (CDC). No splashless, scented or gel bleach (NYS Department of Health).

blocks.warn: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC).

steps: If the well has an electric pump, turn off all electricity and clear debris from around the top of the well.
Repair the electrical system and pump if needed. Get a qualified electrician, well contractor or pump contractor if you are not experienced with this work.

Start the pump and run water until it is clear, from the outside faucet closest to the well, to keep the unsafe water out of the house plumbing. No pump: bail water out of the well with a bucket until it is clear.
If the well feeds the house plumbing, close the valves to any water softener.
Find the amount of bleach in the table for your kind of well below.
In a 5-gallon bucket, mix that bleach with 3 to 5 gallons (12 to 19 liters) of water.

If the bleach and water won’t fit in one bucket, mix and pour it in several batches until all the bleach from the table is in. Don’t use less bleach to make it fit (the app’s reading; CDC does not say).
Drilled or driven well: remove the vent cap and pour the mixture in through a funnel. Bored or dug well: add the mixture to the well. Keep it away from all electrical connections.
Mix it: attach a clean hose to the nearest outside faucet and run water back into the well. No pump: pour water back into the well with a bucket.
Rinse the inside of the well casing with a garden hose or bucket for 5 to 10 minutes.
Open every faucet in the house until you smell a strong chlorine odor at each one, then turn them all off.
Leave the solution in the well and pipes for at least 12 hours.
Then drain it through a hose from an outside faucet onto ground with no plants, such as a driveway, until the chlorine smell is gone. Not into streams, ponds or other open water.
Run all the indoor faucets until the chlorine smell is gone.
Until the water has been tested, boil it (rolling boil for 1 minute) or use other water.

blocks.p: Steps from CDC. NYS Department of Health says to let the well stand preferably 12 to 24 hours, and not to drain the chlorinated water into a septic system or sewer. Above 5,000 ft, boil for 3 minutes (EPA).

With no pump, the faucet steps can’t be done. CDC gives no other no-pump steps; the app’s reading is: let the solution stand in the well at least 12 hours, then bail water out, away from plants and open water, until the chlorine smell is gone. Wear goggles or a face shield while you bail: the water is a strong chlorine solution (CDC).
Bored and dug wells are hard to disinfect: they are shallow and poorly protected, so flood water can carry dirt back in (CDC).

Amounts are approximate, rounded to a practical measure, and give a chlorine level above 100 mg/L. tbsp is tablespoon; 1 cup = 8 fl oz = 16 tbsp; gal is gallon; 1 gallon = 16 cups (CDC). 1 tbsp is about 15 mL, 1 cup about 237 mL, 1 gallon 3.8 L.

list: Wait 7 to 10 days after disinfecting, until every trace of chlorine has been flushed out, then have the water tested (CDC).
Test for total coliform and either E. coli or fecal coliform bacteria (CDC). In New York, use a NY State certified lab and its sterile bottle (NYS Department of Health).
No coliform found: the water can be considered safe to drink. Test again 2 to 4 weeks later and 3 to 4 months later (CDC).
Coliform found: disinfect the well again and test again (CDC).
If you can’t get a test, keep boiling or treating the well water before you drink it.
Springs are fed by shallow groundwater and are easily contaminated. Most springs used for drinking need constant disinfection (Penn State Extension): treat spring water before you drink it.
Fence livestock away from a spring, turn surface water away from it, and keep activities at least 100 feet (30 m) from the spring box (Penn State Extension).
A spring whose flow changes a lot through the year is unreliable and may be contaminated (Penn State Extension).
